strengths: Clear technical presentation of the LMNet architecture with explicit mathematical formulation
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple benchmarks (MMLU, BBH, GSM8K, HumanEval, MBPP, etc.) and datasets
Honest reporting of negative results, such as underperformance on GSM8K with certain models
Demonstrates practical utility for parameter-efficient domain adaptation with limited data (Section 5.2)
Systematic exploration of multiple LMNet variants and integration with existing PEFT methods
Shows that composing pre-trained LLMs with dense communication is technically feasible and can achieve reasonable performance
weaknesses: Central claim about '<0.1% training cost' is fundamentally misleading: only counts edge parameters (~0.01T tokens) while omitting pre-training cost of 0.5B base model (18T tokens). True amortized cost is orders of magnitude higher

Benefits of dense vector communication are not convincingly demonstrated: Section 5.1.2 fails to de-embed intermediate representations; different edge attention patterns show heterogeneity but not effectiveness

Inconsistent experimental results undermine generality: LMNet underperforms prompt-based methods on GSM8K with Qwen models (e.g., 30.93% vs 41.60%), with weak post-hoc explanation that certain models are 'strong enough'
No ablation studies justifying architectural choices: layer-wise fully-connected structure, summation aggregation, single-layer attention blocks are presented without empirical validation

Limited novelty: the approach is primarily architecture design and fine-tuning of pre-trained components, not fundamentally new techniques. Section 5.2 shows LMNet variants don't consistently outperform LoRA despite using more parameters (36.75M vs 0.35M)

Incomplete mechanistic understanding: authors acknowledge inability to de-embed what internal vertices are learning ('outcome input text is not even English'). This directly contradicts claims about 'machine-native communication' and capabilities beyond human heuristics
Experimental limitations acknowledged throughout: 'limited computation budget' caveat repeated multiple times raises concerns about robustness and generalization of results
Missing key comparisons: no comparison with mixture-of-experts, modern ensemble methods, or other multi-agent LLM composition approaches; limited PEFT baselines in Section 5.2
Proposition 1 is trivial: merely states that backpropagation applies to fully-differentiable models, adding no technical insight
Overclaimed contributions: framed as a 'new paradigm for scaling general intelligence' but is primarily limited-data domain adaptation with specific architectural choices, not a fundamental advance

strengths: Clear conceptual motivation for dense vector communication between LLMs
Comprehensive evaluation across multiple standard benchmarks (MMLU, GSM8K, HumanEval, etc.)
Honest acknowledgment of limitations and failure cases (e.g., inability to interpret intermediate dense representations)
Demonstrates application to multiple scenarios: general scaling and domain adaptation
Technically sound forward/backward pass implementation with proper gradient flow
weaknesses: Critical misleading claims about efficiency: the 0.01T training tokens ignore the 18T pre-training tokens of the vertex model; total cost is not <0.1% but similar to baseline models

Fundamentally unfair comparisons: comparing a fine-tuned multi-model system (0.01T additional tokens) against models trained from scratch, without separate ablation showing benefit of dense vectors specifically

Weak experimental results: GSM8K adaptation shows LMNet underperforming prompting baselines (Table 3), E2E results show only marginal improvement over LoRA (70.5 vs 68.9 BLEU), performance inconsistent across benchmarks

Lack of understanding of the proposed method: authors explicitly admit inability to decode intermediate dense representations (Section 5.1.2: 'outcome input text is not even English'), undermining claims about 'machine-native communication' and learned 'roles and protocols'
Missing critical ablation: no direct fine-tuning baseline showing performance gains from dense vector communication specifically versus token-based communication or standard fine-tuning
Limited technical novelty: the approach is essentially parameter-efficient fine-tuning with dense intermediate representations; this is not substantially different from existing adapter/LoRA methods
No comparison with related ensemble/modular LLM approaches, mixture-of-experts, or parameter-efficient fine-tuning literature beyond LoRA
Misleading framing throughout paper: characterized as new 'scaling paradigm' and 'general intelligence' approach when it is parameter-efficient adaptation of a pre-trained model
No inference-time efficiency analysis: claims about dense vector efficiency lack empirical support (FLOPs, memory, latency); unclear if all vertices remain active during inference
Weak theoretical contributions: Proposition 1 is trivial application of chain rule; connection to MLP structure poorly motivated; cognitive science references disconnected from technical choices

strengths: Novel paradigm of direct dense vector communication between LLMs is conceptually interesting and potentially useful
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple benchmarks (MMLU, GSM8K, MATH, HumanEval, etc.) and application scenarios
Clear technical presentation with well-defined mathematical formulation (Sections 3.1-3.2) and sound architectural design
Demonstrates practical utility for model adaptation with limited data and parameter-efficient fine-tuning
Reasonable exploration of different network topologies and training strategies with multiple ablations
weaknesses: Core efficiency claim is misleading: the '<0.1% training cost' refers only to training edge connectors, not the total computation needed to achieve comparable intelligence (vertices already pre-trained with ~18T tokens)

Unfair experimental comparisons in Table 1: comparing LMNet-1B (trained on mixed public data with different schedule) to baseline models trained with distinct data distributions and methodologies, no discussion of data contamination
Cannot interpret intermediate representations to readable text (Section 5.1.2), undermining claims about 'machine-native communication' and the advantages of dense vector representation
Mixed and problematic empirical results: LMNet underperforms simple prompting on GSM8K with strong models (Table 3), suggesting benefits only for weak models and limited scalability

Lack of rigorous validation for core claims: no empirical proof that dense vectors preserve more information than discrete tokens, no ablations comparing to fine-tuning baselines with equivalent compute

Limited technical novelty: removing embedding layers and using attention blocks as adapters is relatively straightforward engineering; related dense communication work is acknowledged but not thoroughly distinguished
Reproducibility concerns: code not provided, missing implementation details (learning rates, schedules, optimizer, hyperparameter selection), training data mixture not precisely specified

Incomplete analysis of interpretability failure: authors acknowledge representations are 'fused' but don't adequately address implications for the proposed mechanism or whether meaningful communication actually occurs

strengths: Clear, well-motivated core insight: removing intermediate embedding/de-embedding layers enables differentiable end-to-end optimization of inter-model communication
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple benchmarks (MMLU, GSM8K, HumanEval, E2E) with reasonable comparisons to test-time scaling and PEFT baselines
Parameter-efficient design through vertex parameter sharing keeps total parameters manageable (1.1B from 0.5B base)
Honest discussion of limitations including when the method fails (e.g., strong models with limited data) and the gap between motivation and implementation
Broad applicability across general capability improvement, downstream task adaptation, reasoning, and coding tasks
Solid empirical results showing ~30.5% relative improvement on benchmarks with <0.2% additional pre-training cost
weaknesses: Critical mismatch between motivation and implementation: paper motivates learning explicit communication protocols for message-passing, but actual implementation uses end-to-end auto-regressive training that produces non-interpretable intermediate representations. Authors acknowledge (Section 6.3) that gains come from test-time computation and learned routing rather than learned communication.

Experimental confounds: LMNet with 14 model copies uses ~14× base computation, similar to 16× Self-Consistency baseline. Improvements not cleanly attributed to dense communication vs. more computation vs. ensemble effects. Missing control comparison with natural-language edges trained end-to-end.

Limited technical novelty: stacking transformers with adapter modules is standard practice. Main contribution (removing embedding layers + end-to-end training) is incremental. Each component exists in prior work.

Shallow analysis of learned communication: macro-level analysis only shows edges differ from initialization; micro-level analysis reveals intermediate vertices produce compressed/filtered outputs without clear communication patterns, contradicting the communication-learning motivation

Context-dependent results weaken generality claims: method underperforms on strong models with limited data (Table 9); requires additional 93.7k training data for GSM8K to work well, contradicting limited-supervision framing; modest improvements on generation tasks (Table 4)

Unjustified architectural choices: topology inspired by MLPs but uses fully-connected DAG (no ablation vs. chains/trees); aggregation by summation chosen for 'simplicity' despite information loss risk; edge module design not ablated. Section 6 discussion lacks empirical validation.

Practical limitations underexplored: requires white-box model access (unlike prompt/API approaches); no actual latency measurements despite O(L×W²) complexity; dense messages less interpretable than natural language
Reproducibility gaps: edge module specifications vary across experiments; training hyperparameters incompletely specified; de-embedding procedure for intermediate analysis not formally described

strengths: Well-motivated problem: Clear articulation of discrete/non-differentiable bottleneck in NL-based LLM communication
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple benchmarks (MMLU, GSM8K, E2E), datasets, and model sizes with ablations
Solid technical execution: Architecture clearly specified with proper mathematical formulation and computational complexity analysis
Honest limitations discussion acknowledging the gap between motivation and actual implementation
Strong empirical results (+30.5% improvement on general reasoning benchmarks) demonstrating practical value
weaknesses: Fundamental motivation-implementation gap: Paper motivates replacing discrete inter-agent NL communication with learned dense protocols, but actually implements end-to-end auto-regressive training through layers, not sentence-by-sentence message passing. Section 6.3 admits this mismatch only in discussion.

Unclear source of improvements: Failed to isolate whether gains come from (a) dense vs. discrete communication, (b) increased depth/parameters, or (c) end-to-end differentiability. Intermediate representations don't decode to meaningful text (Appendix B.2), contradicting the 'learned communication' narrative.

Unfair empirical comparisons: LMNet trained with ~0.02T tokens on data likely in pre-training sets vs. baselines trained with 15-18T tokens. Parameter comparisons conflate model size differences. No actual wall-clock timing despite efficiency claims.

Weak analysis of learned communication: Parameter visualization shows edges differ from random initialization but provides no evidence of semantic meaning. Intermediate nodes fail to produce interpretable messages, suggesting the network learns representational layers rather than true inter-node communication.

Limited practical applicability: Requires white-box access and gradient optimization (unlike NL-based systems), increases inference cost (14 LLM layers + edges vs. single base model), loses interpretability compared to motivating natural-language baseline

Insufficient ablation studies: No justification for single-layer attention blocks, summation aggregation, or layer-wise fully-connected topology. Design choices presented as necessary but never compared to alternatives.

Reproducibility concerns: Code unavailable for review; missing implementation details (learning rates, batch sizes, initialization, exact training procedures); limited GPU-days training makes replication difficult

Gap between stated mechanism and observed behavior: Authors claim 'learning communication protocols' but data shows intermediate representations are opaque. The case study reveals middle-layer outputs don't produce readable text, undermining the communication learning hypothesis.
Parameter sharing restriction: Forced parameter sharing presented as computational necessity but trade-off with specialization never studied; limits model expressiveness
Missing transfer analysis: No evidence that learned edge parameters generalize across domains, model sizes, or task types

strengths: Clear and well-motivated conceptual framework addressing an important problem—dense vs. discrete communication between coordinated LLMs enables gradient-based optimization and learned protocols
Technically sound methodology with proper formulation of end-to-end training, well-justified topology design, and practical complexity reduction via parameter sharing

Comprehensive experimental evaluation across two distinct scenarios (general capability improvement and limited-supervision adaptation) with diverse benchmarks, multiple baseline types, and consistent improvements (+30.5% relative improvement)
Efficient approach requiring only <0.2% of LLM pre-training cost while achieving competitive or superior performance to larger models and test-time scaling methods

Honest and thorough discussion of limitations, including acknowledgment of the gap between motivation (interpretable inter-agent messages) and implementation (end-to-end auto-regressive), with concrete proposals for future work
Meaningful analysis of learned communication patterns showing topology is fully exploited and intermediate vertices exhibit nontrivial behaviors
weaknesses: Gap between motivating vision and actual realization: the paper motivates replacing inter-agent natural-language messages with dense communication, but end-to-end auto-regressive training produces largely uninterpretable intermediate representations, limiting applicability to multi-agent scenarios and reducing the interpretability advantage claimed

Limited insight into what communication protocols are actually learned—macro-level analysis shows edges differ but reveals no clear patterns; micro-level analysis shows de-embedded edge outputs are gibberish; the mechanism underlying improvements remains underspecified

Experimental design conflates multiple variables: LMNet uses 14× model repeats making it difficult to isolate learned-communication benefits from additional inference computation; comparison with Self-Consistency (×16) is not entirely apples-to-apples

Sparse empirical exploration of topology alternatives—only layer-wise fully-connected is tested despite discussion of chains, trees, and sparse graphs; claims about universal approximation are theoretical, not validated experimentally

Missing practical scalability metrics—wall-clock inference time and latency relative to single LLM are unreported; Section 3.3 provides theoretical complexity but practical throughput/latency trade-offs are not demonstrated
Reproducibility concerns including missing code URL and some implementation details (initialization strategies, learning rate schedules, convergence criteria) that could be more explicit

Limited novelty at component level (stripping embedding/de-embedding, seq2seq modules, and MLP-inspired topology are standard); primary contribution is in systems-level combination, which is modest relative to related dense communication work (COCONUT, CODI)
All experiments use relatively small models (0.5B-3B) due to compute constraints; generalization to larger frontier models is unclear despite being the motivating use case
